The typography has a clear point of view and changes with every pack: an arched banner slab, a script brush signature, a Clarendon-like serif with a tracked serif subline, a geometric sans with sunburst, inline deco caps, and a script-plus-heavy-sans pairing for the director card. All of it is period-correct.

The surfaces look real: print grain, foil stripes, slight registration and paper texture. The camera sits tight and cropped on the packs, so it feels like macro footage of real objects and not flat vectors.
Each card has its own palette (royal blue/gold, orange/cream, red/white/blue, mint/green) built from tobacco ad clichés. The variety is deliberate.
Ending on the director credit over a row of filter tips is a good closing card.

The light is flat scanner light on printed surfaces. Directional light, shallow focus or real cellophane and foil highlights would give each pack more physical presence.
The structure repeats (one pack, one name) with no build. A turn or escalation, like B's journey from astrolabe to map to logo, would give it an arc.

tells: A specific, ownable concept: the world is a clockwork map, and cities unfold mechanically from it. The opening is the show's geography lesson.

The materials are rich: engraved brass astrolabe bands with dragon reliefs, carved wood, gears and cogs, and a parchment map with ink rivers. Light is motivated by a central sun, with flares and deep shadow.

The choreography between frames is clear. It goes from a macro band, to a city rising, to a gear-driven Winterfell, to astrolabe rings, to a map with the camera pulled back, to a hero logo inside the ring. There are real changes of scale and weight, and the motion sweeps.
The credits are set small in an engraved Trajan-like serif with house sigils. They are integrated into the map and sit back so the world leads.
The palette is restrained: bronze, umber and slate, which fits the material story.
gaps: The credit typography is serviceable but conventional: a classic Roman inscriptional face, small, with low legibility against busy ground. It has less typographic invention than A or C.
The warm bronze grade across the whole piece is somewhat monochrome. More contrast between regions (cold north, warm south) would sharpen the storytelling.
The logo lockup is a fairly standard flare-and-emblem hero end card, more expected than the inventive frames before it.

tells: The silhouette-chase idea comes from the source comic and Saul Bass/60s caper titles but is fully owned. Each credit is a set-piece gag: a spiral vortex, a moon-chase, a rocket glimpsed behind the figures.

The colour is bold and uncommon, with a different palette per scene: dusty rose, teal and ochre, violet night, acid chartreuse, peach and black, petrol blue. The silhouettes are recoloured to match each scene.
The compositions vary widely: a wide establishing gate, a top-down alley lit by a pool of lamp light, a graphic concentric spiral, a full-moon profile. Every frame works as a poster.
The illustrated sans type is hand-drawn and integrated into the scenes: on the gate sign, in the alley as a pavement light pool, in perspective.
Paper grain and slightly irregular edges give the flat graphics texture. Cast shadows and lamp light give depth.
gaps: The later credit cards fall back on plain stacked sans titles laid over the scene. A's typographic invention per card would lift them.
Some shapes, like the clouds and background buildings, are cleaner and more vector-default than the hero silhouettes. The texture could be pushed further.
Light is graphic and not physical. A few moments of the real materiality and depth B achieves would give a contrast beat.

defects: The environment looks like a greybox: the buildings are untextured, low-poly blocks with flat emissive window cards. The street reads as previs, not a finished world.
Blacks are crushed through most frames. Frames 3 and 4 are mostly empty dark mass, and the street gives almost no bounce light or wet-surface response to the signs.
Background signs overlap and clip. 'SAUL KIM' sits behind 'KENJI ARAMAKI' and 'K / VIST' is cut off at the left edge, so distant names are unreadable mush rather than a deliberate depth layer.
The 'WRITTEN & DIRECTED BY' card is soft and smeared in its second frame. The blur reads as a stepped, low-sample motion blur, not a clean camera-shutter blur.
The 'KOVÁČ' frame is cropped so tightly to the sign that the camera move ends in a flat, poster-less composition with a stray grey card poking in at the top.
The end title holds about 3.4 s with almost no change between the paired frames. The only life is the RGB split and a slight drift, so it reads as dead air rather than a settle.
The RGB split / chromatic fringing on the title is a generic glitch overlay and is applied unevenly ('N' and 'T' get heavy fringing, the rest are clean).

Typefaces are inconsistent across the credit signs: a condensed grotesk, a slab, a script serif on 'Lev Ansari', and a small geometric sans. It reads as default font variety rather than a casting system.
gaps: Motion: one camera device is repeated (a dolly or whip down the street past a sign) with no change of lens, height or speed profile, and nothing in the world reacts to the camera. Top studio work would vary the choreography, for example signs flickering on in sequence or light spilling onto the street as names land, and would earn the final hold with a real settle move instead of a static lock-off.

Sound: the spectrogram shows sparse, evenly spaced clicks over a thin low tonal bed with few static partials, then a generic white-noise riser (about 6.5–8.5 s) into a drop. There is no evidence of foley that places us in a street (buzzing neon, hum, footsteps, ambience) or of the 'chorus' the title promises. It reads as a stock riser-and-hit pattern, not designed sound.

Finish: the halftone and line-screen treatment in the title crop is the strongest material in the piece, but the world around it is unlit greybox. Without textured facades, wet ground reflections, volumetric haze or real light falloff from the signs, the frames don't hold as posters, and the 'night street' premise is stated rather than rendered.
